Divided Differences

Carl de Boor

21 December 2004

“Est enim fere ex pulcherrimis quæ solvere desiderem.”

(It is among the most beautiful I could desire to solve.) [ citN76 ]

Abstract. Starting with a novel definition of divided differences, this essay derives and discusses the basic properties of, and facts about, (univariate) divided differences.

1   Introduction and basic facts

While there are several ways to think of divided differences, including the one suggested by their very name, the most efficient way is as the coefficients in a Newton form. This form provides an efficient representation of Hermite interpolants.

Let Π⊂(I​F→I​F)\Pi\subset({{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}\to{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}) be the linear space of polynomials in one real (IF=I​R{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}={\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.99997pt{\rm R}}\nolimits}) or complex (I​F=C​ {{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}={\rm C\kern-5.12128pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=6.0pt,depth=-0.2pt\kern 5.12128pt}) variable, and let Π<n\Pi_{<n} denote the subspace of all polynomials of degree <n<n. The Newton form of p∈Πp\in\Pi with respect to the sequence t=(t1,t2,…)t=(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots) of centers tjt_{j} is its expansion

p=:∑j=1∞wj−1,t​c​(j)p=:\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}w_{j-1,t}\,c(j)\immediate (1)

in terms of the Newton polynomials

wi:=wi,t:=(⋅−t1)⋯(⋅−ti),i=0,1,….w_{i}\;:=\;w_{i,t}\;:=\;(\cdot-t_{1})\cdots(\cdot-t_{i}),\quad i=0,1,\ldots\;.\immediate (2)

Each p∈Πp\in\Pi does, indeed, have exactly one such expansion for any given tt since deg⁡wj,t=j\deg w_{j,t}=j, all jj, hence (wj−1,t:j∈I​N)(w_{j-1,t}:j\in{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.99997pt{\rm N}}\nolimits}) is a graded basis for Π\Pi in the sense that, for each nn, (wj−1,t:j=1:n)(w_{j-1,t}:j=1{:}n) is a basis for Π<n\Pi_{<n}.

In other words, the column map

Wt:I​F0I​N→Π:c↦∑j=1∞wj−1,t​c​(j)W_{t}:{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}_{0}^{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.63885pt{\rm N}}\nolimits}\to\Pi:c\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}w_{j-1,t}c(j)\immediate (3)

(from the space I​F0I​N{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}_{0}^{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.63885pt{\rm N}}\nolimits} of scalar sequences with finitely many nonzero entries to the space Π\Pi) is 1-1 and onto, hence invertible. In particular, for each n∈I​Nn\in{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.99997pt{\rm N}}\nolimits}, the coefficient c⁡(n)c(n) in the Newton form (1) for pp depends linearly on pp, i.e., p↦c⁡(n)=(Wt−1​p)​(n)p\mapsto c(n)=(W_{t}^{-1}p)(n) is a well-defined linear functional on Π\Pi, and vanishes on Π<n−1\Pi_{<n-1}. More than that, since all the (finitely many nontrivial) terms in (1) with j>nj>n have wn,tw_{n,t} as a factor, we can write

p=pn+wn,t​qn,p\;=\;p_{n}+w_{n,t}q_{n},\immediate (4)

with qnq_{n} a polynomial we will look at later (in Example 6), and with

pn:=∑j=1nwj−1,t​c​(j)p_{n}\;:=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j-1,t}c(j)

a polynomial of degree <n<n. This makes pnp_{n} necessarily the remainder left by the division of pp by wn,tw_{n,t}, hence well-defined for every nn, hence, by induction, we obtain another proof that the Newton form (1) itself is well-defined.

In particular, pnp_{n} depends only on pp and on

t1:n:=(t1,…,tn),t_{1:n}:=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}),

therefore the same is true of its leading coefficient, c⁡(n)c(n). This is reflected in the (implicit) definition

p=:∑j=1∞wj−1,t ​Δ(t1:j)p,p∈Π,p\;=:\;\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}w_{j-1,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})p,\quad p\in\Pi,\immediate (5)

in which the coefficient c⁡(j)c(j) in the Newton form (1) for pp is denoted

 ​Δ(t1:j)p= ​Δ(t1,…,tj)p:=((Wt)−1p)(j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})p\;=\;\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{j})p\;:=\;((W_{t})^{-1}p)(j)\immediate (6)

and called the divided difference of pp at t1,…,tjt_{1},\ldots,t_{j}. It is also called a divided difference of order j−1j-1, and the reason for all this terminology will be made clear in a moment.

Since WtW_{t} is a continuous function of tt, so is Wt−1W_{t}^{-1}, hence so is  ​Δ(t1:j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}) (see Proposition  label:propcont  for proof details). Further, since wj,tw_{j,t} is symmetric in t1,…,tjt_{1},\ldots,t_{j}, so is  ​Δ(t1:j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}). Also,  ​Δ(t1:j)⟂Π<j\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})\perp\Pi_{<j} (as mentioned before).

In more practical terms, we have

Proposition 7

The sum

pn=∑j=1nwj−1,t ​Δ(t1:j)pp_{n}\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j-1,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})p

of the first nn terms in the Newton form (1) for pp is the Hermite interpolant to pp at t1:nt_{1:n}, i.e., the unique polynomial rr of degree <n<n that agrees with pp at t1:nt_{1:n} in the sense that

Di​r​(z)=Di​p​(z),0≤i<μz:=#⁡{j∈[1..n]:tj=z},z∈I​F.D^{i}r(z)=D^{i}p(z),\quad 0\leq i<\mu_{z}:=\#\{j\in[1\mathbin{\mathchar 24890\relax\mathchar 24890\relax}n]:t_{j}=z\},\quad z\in{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}.\immediate (8)

Proof: One readily verifies by induction on the nonnegative integer μ\mu that, for any z∈I​Fz\in{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}, any polynomial ff vanishes μ\mu-fold at zz iff ff has (⋅−z)μ(\cdot-z)^{\mu} as a factor, i.e.,

Dif(z)=0 for i=0,…,μ−1⟺f∈(⋅−z)μΠ.D^{i}f(z)=0\hbox{\ \ for\ \ }i=0,\ldots,\mu-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\in(\cdot-z)^{\mu}\Pi.\immediate (9)

Since p−pn=wn,t​qnp-p_{n}=w_{n,t}q_{n}, this implies that r=pnr=p_{n} does, indeed satisfy (8).

Also, pnp_{n} is the only such polynomial since, by (9), for any polynomial rr satisfying (8), the difference pn−rp_{n}-r must have wnw_{n} as a factor and, if rr is of degree <n<n, then this is possible only when r=pnr=p_{n}.       

Example 1. For n=1n=1, we get that

 ​Δ​(t1):p↦p⁡(t1),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1}):p\mapsto p(t_{1}),

i.e.,  ​Δ​(τ)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau) can serve as a (nonstandard) notation for the linear functional of evaluation at τ\tau.      

Example 2. For n=2n=2, pnp_{n} is the polynomial of degree <2<2 that matches pp at t1:2t_{1:2}. If t1≠t2t_{1}\not=t_{2}, then we know p2p_{2} to be writable in ‘point-slope form’ as

p2=p(t1)+(⋅−t1)p⁡(t2)−p⁡(t1)t2−t1,p_{2}=p(t_{1})+(\cdot-t_{1}){p(t_{2})-p(t_{1})\over t_{2}-t_{1}},

while if t1=t2t_{1}=t_{2}, then we know p2p_{2} to be

p2=p(t1)+(⋅−t1)Dp(t1).p_{2}=p(t_{1})+(\cdot-t_{1})Dp(t_{1}).

Hence, altogether,

 ​Δ(t1:2)p={p⁡(t2)−p⁡(t1)t2−t1,t1≠t2;D​p​(t1),otherwise.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:2})p\;=\;\cases{{\displaystyle p(t_{2})-p(t_{1})\over\displaystyle\mathstrut t_{2}-t_{1}},&$t_{1}\not=t_{2}$;\cr\vskip 4.0pt\cr Dp(t_{1}),&otherwise.\cr}\immediate (10)

Thus, for t1≠t2t_{1}\not=t_{2},  ​Δ(t1:2)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:2}) is a quotient of differences, i.e., a divided difference.      

Example 3. Directly from the definition of the divided difference,

 ​Δ(t1:j)wi−1,t=δj​i,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})w_{i-1,t}=\delta_{ji},\immediate (11)

therefore (remembering that  ​Δ(t1:j)⟂Π<j−1\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})\perp\Pi_{<j-1})

 ​Δ(t1:j)()j−1= 1,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})()^{j-1}\;=\;1,\immediate (12)

with

()k:I​F→I​F:z↦zk()^{k}:{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}\to{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}:z\mapsto z^{k}

a handy if nonstandard notation for the power functions.       

Example 4. If tt is a constant sequence, t=(τ,τ,…)t=(\tau,\tau,\ldots) say, then

wj,(τ,τ,…)=(⋅−τ)j,w_{j,(\tau,\tau,\ldots)}=(\cdot-\tau)^{j},

hence the Taylor expansion

p=∑n=0∞(⋅−τ)nDnp(τ)/n!p=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(\cdot-\tau)^{n}D^{n}p(\tau)/n!\immediate (13)

is the Newton form for the polynomial pp with respect to the sequence (τ,τ,…)(\tau,\tau,\ldots). Therefore,

 ​Δ(τ[n+1])p:= ​Δ(τ,…,τ⏟n+1​terms)p=Dnp(τ)/n!,n=0,1,….\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau^{[n+1]})p:=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\underbrace{\tau,\ldots,\tau}_{n+1\,\rm terms})p=D^{n}p(\tau)/n!,\quad n=0,1,\ldots\,.\immediate (14)

      

Example 5. If ℓ:t↦a​t+b\ell:t\mapsto at+b, then (ℓ⁡(z)−ℓ⁡(ti))=a⁡(z−ti)(\ell(z)-\ell(t_{i}))=a(z-t_{i}), hence

an−1 ​Δ(ℓ(t1:n))p= ​Δ(t1:n)(p∘ℓ).a^{n-1}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\ell(t_{1:n}))p=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}n})(p\circ\ell).\immediate (15)

      

Example 6. Consider the polynomial qnq_{n} introduced in (4):

p=pn+wn,t​qn.p=p_{n}+w_{n,t}q_{n}.

Since p⁡(tn+1)=pn+1​(tn+1)p(t_{n+1})=p_{n+1}(t_{n+1}) and pn+1=pn+wn,t ​Δ(t1:n+1)pp_{n+1}=p_{n}+w_{n,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n+1})p, we have

wn,t(tn+1)qn(tn+1)=wn,t(tn+1) ​Δ(t1:n+1)p,w_{n,t}(t_{n+1})q_{n}(t_{n+1})=w_{n,t}(t_{n+1})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n+1})p,

therefore

qn(tn+1)= ​Δ(t1:n+1)p,q_{n}(t_{n+1})=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n+1})p,

at least for any tn+1t_{n+1} for which wn,t​(tn+1)≠0w_{n,t}(t_{n+1})\not=0, hence for every tn+1∈I​Ft_{n+1}\in{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}, by the continuity of qnq_{n}, and the continuity of  ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)p\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}n},\cdot)p, i.e., of  ​Δ(t1:n+1)p\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}n+1})p as a function of tn+1t_{n+1}. It follows that

qn= ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)pq_{n}=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n},\cdot)p

and

p=pn+wn,t ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)p,p=p_{n}+w_{n,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n},\cdot)p,\immediate (16)

the standard error formula for Hermite interpolation. More than that, by the very definition, (4), of qnq_{n}, we now know that

 ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)p=qn=(p−pn)/wn,t=∑j>nwj−1,twn,t ​Δ(t1:j)p,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n},\cdot)p\;=\;q_{n}=(p-p_{n})/w_{n,t}=\sum_{j>n}{w_{j-1,t}\over w_{n,t}}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})p,\immediate (17)

and we recognize the sum here as a Newton form with respect to the sequence (tj:j>n)(t_{j}:j>n). This provides us with the following basic divided difference identity:

 ​Δ(tn+1:j) ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)= ​Δ(t1:j),j>n.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{n+1:j})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n},\cdot)=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}),\quad j>n.\immediate (18)

      

For the special case n=j−2n=j-2, the basic divided difference identity, (18), reads

 ​Δ(tj−1:j) ​Δ(t1:j−2,⋅)= ​Δ(t1:j),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j-1:j})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j-2},\cdot)=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}),

or, perhaps more suggestively,

 ​Δ(tj−1,⋅) ​Δ(t1:j−2,⋅)= ​Δ(t1:j−1,⋅),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j-1},\cdot)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j-2},\cdot)=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j-1},\cdot),

hence, by induction,

 ​Δ(tj−1,⋅) ​Δ(tj−2,⋅)⋯ ​Δ(t1,⋅)= ​Δ(t1:j−1,⋅).\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j-1},\cdot)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j-2},\cdot)\,\cdots\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1},\cdot)\;=\;\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j-1},\cdot).\immediate (19)

In other words,  ​Δ(t1:j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}) is obtainable by forming difference quotients j−1j-1 times. This explains our calling  ​Δ(t1:j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}) a ‘divided difference of order j−1j-1’.

2   Continuity and smoothness

The column map

Wt:I​F0I​N→Π:c↦∑j=1∞wj−1,t​c​(j)W_{t}:{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}_{0}^{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.63885pt{\rm N}}\nolimits}\to\Pi:c\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}w_{j-1,t}c(j)

introduced in (3) is continuous as a function of tt, hence so is its inverse, as follows directly from the identity

A−1−B−1=A−1​(B−A)​B−1,A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1},\immediate (20)

valid for any two invertible maps AA, BB (with the same domain and target). Therefore, also each  ​Δ(t1:j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}) is a continuous function of tt, all of this in the pointwise sense. Here is the formal statement and its proof.

Proposition 21

For any p∈Πp\in\Pi,

lims→t( ​Δ(s1:j)p:j∈I​N)=( ​Δ(t1:j)p:j∈I​N).\lim_{s\to t}(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:j})p:j\in{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.99997pt{\rm N}}\nolimits})=(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})p:j\in{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.99997pt{\rm N}}\nolimits}).

Proof: Let p∈Π<np\in\Pi_{<n}. Then t↦ ​Δ(t1:k)p=0t\mapsto\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}k})p=0 for k>nk>n, hence trivially continuous. As for k≤nk\leq n, let

Wt,n:=I​Fn→Π<n:c↦∑j=1nwj−1,t​c​(j)W_{t,n}:={{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}^{n}\to\Pi_{<n}:c\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j-1,t}c(j)

be the restriction of WtW_{t} to I​Fn{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}^{n}, as a linear map to Π<n\Pi_{<n}. Then, in whatever norms we might choose on I​Fn{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}^{n} and Π<n\Pi_{<n}, Wt,nW_{t,n} is bounded and invertible, hence boundedly invertible uniformly in t1:nt_{1:n} as long as t1:nt_{1:n} lies in some bounded set. Therefore, with (20), since lims→tWs,n=Wt,n\lim_{s\to t}W_{s,n}=W_{t,n}, also

lims→t( ​Δ(s1:j)p:j=1:n)=(Wt,n)−1p=( ​Δ(t1:j)p:j=1:n).\lim_{s\to t}(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:j})p:j=1{:}n)=(W_{t,n})^{-1}p=(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})p:j=1{:}n).

      

This continuity is very useful. For example, it implies that it is usually sufficient to check a proposed divided difference identity by checking it only for pairwise distinct arguments.

As another example, we used the continuity earlier (in Example 6) to prove that  ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)p\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}n},\cdot)p is a polynomial. This implies that  ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)p\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}n},\cdot)p is differentiable, and, with that, (18) and (14) even provide the following formula for the derivatives.

Proposition 22
Dk ​Δ(t1:j,⋅)p=k! ​Δ(t1:j,[⋅]k+1)p,k∈I​N.D^{k}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j},\cdot)p=k!\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j},[\cdot]^{k+1})p,\quad k\in{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.99997pt{\rm N}}\nolimits}.

3   Refinement

Already Cauchy [ citCa ] had occasion to use the simplest nontrivial case of the following fact.

Proposition 23

For any nn-sequence tt and any 1≤σ⁡(1)<⋯<σ⁡(k)≤n1\leq\sigma(1)<\cdots<\sigma(k)\leq n,

 ​Δ(tσ⁡(1:k))=∑j=σ⁡(1)−1σ⁡(k)−kα(j) ​Δ(tj+1:j+k),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{\sigma(1:k)})=\sum_{j=\sigma(1)-1}^{\sigma(k)-k}\alpha(j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j+1:j+k}),

with α=αt,σ\alpha=\alpha_{t,\sigma} positive in case tt is strictly increasing.

Proof: Since  ​Δ(t1:n)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n}) is symmetric in the tjt_{j}, (18) implies

(tn−t1)( ​Δ(t1:n\m)− ​Δ(t2:n))=(t1−tm)( ​Δ(t2:n)− ​Δ(t1:n−1)),(t_{n}-t_{1})(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n\backslash m})-\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{2:n}))\;=\;(t_{1}-t_{m})(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{2:n})-\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n-1})),

with

t1:n\m:=t1:m−1,m+1:n:=(t1,…,tm−1,tm+1,…,tn).t_{1{:}n\backslash m}:=t_{1{:}m-1,m+1{:}n}:=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m-1},t_{m+1},\ldots,t_{n}).

On rearranging the terms, we get

(tn−t1) ​Δ(t1:n\m)=(tn−tm) ​Δ(t2:n)+(tm−t1) ​Δ(t1:n−1),(t_{n}-t_{1})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n\backslash m})\;=\;(t_{n}-t_{m})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{2:n})+(t_{m}-t_{1})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n-1}),

and this proves the assertion for the special case k=n−1k=n-1, and even gives an explicit formula for α\alpha in this case.

From this, the general case follows by induction on n−kn-k, with α\alpha computable as a convolution of sequences which, by induction, are positive in case tt is strictly increasing (since this is then trivially so for k=n−1k=n-1), hence then α\alpha itself is positive.       

My earliest reference for the general case is [ citP33 ].

4   Divided difference of a product: Leibniz, Opitz

The map

P:=Pn,t:Π→Π:p↦pn,P:=P_{n,t}:\Pi\to\Pi:p\mapsto p_{n},

of Hermite interpolation at t1:nt_{1:n}, is the linear projector PP on Π\Pi with

ranP=Π<n,ran(id−P)=nullP=wt,n​Π.\mathop{\rm ran}\nolimits P=\Pi_{<n},\quad\mathop{\rm ran}\nolimits({\rm id}-P)=\mathop{\rm null}\nolimits P=w_{t,n}\Pi.

In particular, the nullspace of PP is an ideal if, as we may, we think of Π\Pi as a ring, namely the ring with multiplication defined pointwise,

(p​g)​(z):=p⁡(z)​g​(z),z∈I​F.(pg)(z):=p(z)g(z),\quad z\in{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}.

In other words, the nullspace of PP is a linear subspace closed also under pointwise multiplication. This latter fact is (see [ citB03b ]) equivalent to the identity

P⁡(p​q)=P⁡(p⁡(P​q)),p,q∈Π.P(pq)=P(p(Pq)),\quad p,q\in\Pi.\immediate (24)

For p∈Πp\in\Pi, consider the map

Mp:Π<n→Π<n:f↦P⁡(p​f).M_{p}:\Pi_{<n}\to\Pi_{<n}:f\mapsto P(pf).

Then MpM_{p} is evidently linear and, also evidently, so is the resulting map

M:Π→L⁡(Π<n):p↦MpM:\Pi\to L(\Pi_{<n}):p\mapsto M_{p}

on Π\Pi to the space of linear maps on Π<n\Pi_{<n}. More than that, since, by (24),

Mp​qf=P(pqf)=P(pP(qf))=MpMqf,p∈Π<n,p,q∈Π,M_{pq}f=P(pqf)=P(pP(qf))=M_{p}M_{q}f,\quad p\in\Pi_{<n},\;p,q\in\Pi,

MM is a ring homomorphism, from the ring Π\Pi into the ring L⁡(Π<n)L(\Pi_{<n}) in which composition serves as multiplication. The latter ring is well known not to be commutative while, evidently, ranM\mathop{\rm ran}\nolimits M is a commutative subring.

It follows, in particular, that

Mp=p⁡(M()1),p∈Π,M_{p}=p(M_{()^{1}}),\quad p\in\Pi,

hence

Mp^=p⁡(M()1^),p∈Π,\widehat{M_{p}}=p(\widehat{M_{()^{1}}}),\quad p\in\Pi,

for the matrix representation

Mp^:=V​Mp​V−1\widehat{M_{p}}:=VM_{p}V^{-1}

of MpM_{p} with respect to any particular basis VV of Π<n\Pi_{<n}. Look, in particular, at the matrix representation with respect to the Newton basis

V:=[wj−1,t:j=1:n]V:=[w_{j-1,t}:j=1{:}n]

for Π<n\Pi_{<n}. Since

()1wj−1,t=tjwj−1,t+wj,t,j=1,2,…,()^{1}w_{j-1,t}=t_{j}w_{j-1,t}+w_{j,t},\quad j=1,2,\ldots,

therefore evidently

M()1​wj−1,t=P⁡(()1​wj−1,t)=tj​wj−1,t+(1−δj,n)​wj,t,j=1:n.M_{()^{1}}w_{j-1,t}=P(()^{1}w_{j-1,t})=t_{j}w_{j-1,t}+(1-\delta_{j,n})w_{j,t},\quad j=1{:}n.

M()1^=An,t:=[t11t21t3⋱⋱1tn].\widehat{M_{()^{1}}}\;=\;A_{n,t}\;:=\;\left[\matrix{t_{1}&&&&\cr 1&t_{2}&&&\cr&1&t_{3}&&\cr&&\ddots&\ddots&\cr&&&1&t_{n}\cr}\right].

On the other hand, for any p∈Πp\in\Pi and j=1:nj=1{:}n,

(∑i=jn(wi−1,t/wj−1,t) ​Δ(tj:i)p)wj−1,t\left(\sum_{i=j}^{n}(w_{i-1,t}/w_{j-1,t})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})p\right)w_{j-1,t}

is a polynomial of degree <n<n and, for pairwise distinct tit_{i}, it agrees with p​wj−1,tpw_{j-1,t} at t1:nt_{1:n} since the sum describes the polynomial of degree ≤n−j\leq n-j that matches pp at tj:nt_{j:n} while both functions vanish at t1:j−1t_{1:j-1}. we conclude that

at least when the tit_{i} are pairwise distinct. In other words, the jjth column of the matrix Mp^=V−1​Mp​V\widehat{M_{p}}=V^{-1}M_{p}V (which represents MpM_{p} with respect to the Newton basis VV for Π<n\Pi_{<n}) has the entries

( ​Δ(tj:i)p:i=1:n)=(0,…,0,p(tj), ​Δ(tj,tj+1)p,…, ​Δ(tj:n)p).(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})p:i=1{:}n)=(0,\ldots,0,p(t_{j}),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j},t_{j+1})p,\ldots,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j{:}n})p).

By the continuity of the divided difference (see Proposition 21), this implies

Proposition 25: Opitz formula

For any p∈Πp\in\Pi,

p(An,t)=( ​Δ(tj:i)p:i,j=1:n).p(A_{n,t})\;=\;(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})p:i,j=1{:}n).\immediate (26)

The remarkable identity (26) is due to G. Opitz; see [ citO ] which records a talk announced but not delivered. Opitz calls the matrices p⁡(An,t)p(A_{n,t}) Steigungsmatrizen (‘difference-quotient matrices’). Surprisingly, Opitz explicitly excludes the possibility that some of the tjt_{j} might coincide. [ citBR ] ascribe (26) to Sylvester, but I have been unable to locate anything like this formula in Sylvester’s collected works.

Example 7. For the monomial ()k()^{k}, Opitz’ formula gives

 ​Δ(t1:n)()k=(An,t)k(n,1)=∑ν∈{1:n}kAn,t(n,νk)An,t(νk,νk−1)⋯An,t(ν1,1),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})()^{k}=(A_{n,t})^{k}(n,1)=\sum_{\nu\in\{1{:}n\}^{k}}A_{n,t}(n,\nu_{k})A_{n,t}(\nu_{k},\nu_{k-1})\cdots A_{n,t}(\nu_{1},1),

and, since An,tA_{n,t} is bidiagonal, the ν\nuth summand is zero unless the sequence (1,ν1,…,νk,n)(1,\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{k},n) is increasing, with any strict increase no bigger than 1, in which case the summand equals tαt^{\alpha}, with αj−1\alpha_{j}-1 the multiplicity with which jj appears in the sequence ν\nu, j=1:nj=1{:}n. This confirms that  ​Δ(t1:n)()k=0\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})()^{k}=0 for k<n−1k<n-1 and proves that

 ​Δ(t1:n)()k=∑|α|=k−n−1tα,k≥n−1.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})()^{k}=\sum_{|\alpha|=k-n-1}t^{\alpha},\quad k\geq n-1.\immediate (27)

      

My first reference for (27) is [ citSt27 : p.19f]. To be sure, once (27) is known, it is easily verified by induction, using the Leibniz formula, to be derived next.

Since, for any square matrix AA and any polynomials pp and qq,

(p​q)​(A)=p​(A)​q​(A),(pq)(A)=p(A)q(A),

it follows, in particular, that

 ​Δ(t1:n)(pq)=Mp​q^(n,1)=Mp^(n,:)Mq^(:,1),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})(pq)=\widehat{M_{pq}}(n,1)=\widehat{M_{p}}(n,:)\widehat{M_{q}}(:,1),

hence

Corollary 28: Leibniz formula

For any p,q∈Πp,q\in\Pi,

 ​Δ(t1:n)(pq)=∑j=1:n ​Δ(tj:n)p ​Δ(t1:j)q.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})(pq)=\sum_{j=1:n}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:n})p\;\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})q.\immediate (29)

On the other hand, the Leibniz formula implies that, for any p,q∈Πp,q\in\Pi,

( ​Δ(tj:i)p:i,j=1:n)( ​Δ(tj:i)q:i,j=1:n)=( ​Δ(tj:i)(pq):i,j=1:n),(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})p:i,j=1{:}n)(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})q:i,j=1{:}n)\;=\;(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})(pq):i,j=1{:}n),

hence, that, for any p∈Πp\in\Pi,

p(( ​Δ(tj:i)()1:i,j=1:n))=( ​Δ(tj:i)p:i,j=1:n).p((\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})()^{1}:i,j=1{:}n))\;=\;(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j:i})p:i,j=1{:}n).

In other words, we can also view Opitz’ formula as a corollary to Leibniz’ formula.

My first reference for the Leibniz formula is [ citP33 ], though Steffensen later devotes an entire paper, [ citSt39 ], to it and this has become the standard reference for it despite the fact that Popoviciu, in response, wrote his own overview of divided differences, [ citP40 ], trying, in vain, to correct the record.

The (obvious) name ‘Leibniz formula’ for it appears first in [ citB72 ].

Induction on mm proves the following

Corollary 30: General Leibniz formula

For f:I​Fm→I​Ff:{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}^{m}\to{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}},

 ​Δ(t1,…,tk)f(⋅,…,⋅)=∑1=i⁡(1)≤⋯≤i⁡(m)=k(⊗j=1m ​Δ(ti⁡(j−1),…,ti⁡(j)))f.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})f(\cdot,\ldots,\cdot)=\sum_{1=i(1)\leq\cdots\leq i(m)=k}\left(\otimes_{j=1}^{m}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{i(j-1)},\ldots,t_{i(j)})\right)f.

Assume that the sequence (t1,…,tn)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) has all its multiplicities (if any) clustered, meaning that, for any i<ji<j, ti=tjt_{i}=t_{j} implies that ti=ti+1=⋯=tjt_{i}=t_{i+1}=\cdots=t_{j}. Then, by (18) and (14),

 ​Δ(ti:j)p={Δ(ti+1:j)p−Δ(ti:j−1)ptj−ti,ti≠tj;Dj−i​p​(ti)/(j−i)!otherwise,1≤i≤j≤n.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{i:j})p\;=\;\cases{{{\displaystyle\mathstrut\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{i+1:j})p-\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{i:j-1})p}\over{\displaystyle\mathstrut t_{j}-t_{i}}},&$t_{i}\not=t_{j}$;\cr\vskip 3.0pt\cr D^{j-i}p(t_{i})/(j-i)!&otherwise,\cr}\quad 1\leq i\leq j\leq n.

column by column from left to right, using one of the nn pieces of information

Proposition 32

Let (t1,…,tn)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) have all its multiplicities (if any) clustered, and let y∈I​Fny\in{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}^{n} be arbitrary. 6   Evaluation of a Newton form via Horner’s method

Horner’s method

Let c(j):= ​Δ(t1:j)rc(j):=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})r for j=1,…,n>deg⁡rj=1,\ldots,n>\deg r, z∈I​Fz\in{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}, and

c^​(n):=c⁡(n),c^​(j):=c(j)+(z−tj)c^(j+1),j=n−1,n−2,…,1.\eqalign{\widehat{c}(n)&:=c(n),\cr\widehat{c}(j)&:=c(j)+(z-t_{j})\widehat{c}(j+1),\quad j=n{-}1,n{-}2,\ldots,1.\cr}

Then c^​(1)=r​(z)\widehat{c}(1)=r(z). More than that,

r=∑j=1nwj−1,t^​c^​(j),r=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j-1,\widehat{t}\ }\widehat{c}(j),

with

t^:=(z,t1,t2,…).\widehat{t}\;:=\;(z,t_{1},t_{2},\ldots).

Proof: The first claim follows from the second, or else directly from the fact that Horner’s method is nothing but the evaluation, from the inside out, of the nested expression

r⁡(z)=c⁡(1)+(z−t1)​(c⁡(2)+⋯+(z−tn−2)​(c⁡(n−1)+(z−tn−1)​c​(n))+⋯),r(z)=c(1)+(z-t_{1})(c(2)+\cdots+(z-t_{n-2})(c(n-1)+(z-t_{n-1})c(n))\cdots),

for which reason Horner’s method is also known as Nested Multiplication.

As to the second claim, note that  ​Δ(z,t1:n−1)r= ​Δ(t1:n)r\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z,t_{1:n-1})r=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})r since deg⁡r<n\deg r<n, hence c^(n)= ​Δ(z,t1:n−1)r\widehat{c}(n)=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z,t_{1:n-1})r, while, directly from (18),

 ​Δ(⋅,t1:j−1)= ​Δ(t1:j)+(⋅−tj) ​Δ(⋅,t1:j),j∈I​N,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\cdot,t_{1:j-1})=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})+(\cdot-t_{j})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\cdot,t_{1:j}),\quad j\in{\mathop{{\rm I}\kern-1.99997pt{\rm N}}\nolimits},\immediate (34)

hence, by (downward) induction,

c^(j)= ​Δ(z,t1:j−1)r,j=n−1,n−2,…,1.\widehat{c}(j)=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z,t_{1:j-1})r,\quad j=n{-}1,n{-}2,\ldots,1.

      

In effect, Horner’s Method is another way of filling in a divided difference table, starting not at the left-most column but with a diagonal, and generating new entries, not from left to right, but from right to left:

Δ​(z)​rΔ​(z,t1)​rΔ​(t1)​rΔ(z,t1:2)rΔ(t1:2)r⋅⋅Δ(t1:3)rΔ(z,t1:n−2)r⋅⋅Δ(z,t1:n−1)r=Δ(t1:n)r⋅⋅Δ(t1:n−1)r⋅⋅Δ(t1:n)r⋅⋅⋅\matrix{\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z)r&&&&\cr&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z,t_{1})r&&&\cr\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1})r&&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z,t_{1:2})r&&\cr&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:2})r&&\ \ \ \cdot\ \ \ &\cr\cdot&&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:3})r&&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z,t_{1:n-2})r\cr&\cdot&&\ \ \ \cdot\ \ \ &&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z,t_{1:n-1})r=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})r\cr\cdot&&\cdot&&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n-1})r&\cr&\cdot&&\ \ \ \cdot\ \ \ &&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})r\cr\cdot&&\ \ \ \cdot\ \ \ &&\cdot&\cr}

Hence, Horner’s method is useful for carrying out a change of basis, going from one Newton form to another. Specifically, n−1n-1-fold iteration of this process, with z=zn−1,…,z1z=z_{n-1},\ldots,z_{1}, is an efficient way of computing the coefficients ( ​Δ(z1:j)r:j=1,…,n)(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z_{1:j})r:j=1,\ldots,n), of the Newton form for r∈Π<nr\in\Pi_{<n} with respect to the centers z1:n−1z_{1:n-1}, from those for the Newton form with respect to centers t1:n−1t_{1:n-1}. Not all the steps need actually be carried out in case all the zjz_{j} are the same, i.e., when switching to the Taylor form (or local power form).

7   Divided differences of functions other than polynomials

Proposition 35

On Π\Pi, the divided differences  ​Δ(t1:j)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}), j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, provide a basis for the linear space of linear functionals spanned by

 ​Δ​(tj)​Dμj,μj:=#⁡{i<j:ti=tj};j=1,…,n.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j})D^{\mu_{j}},\quad\mu_{j}:=\#\{i<j:t_{i}=t_{j}\};\quad j=1,\ldots,n.\immediate (36)

Proof: By Proposition 7 and its proof,

∩j=1nker ​Δ(t1:j)=wn,tΠ=∩j=1nker ​Δ(tj)Dμj.\cap_{j=1}^{n}\ker\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})=w_{n,t}\Pi=\cap_{j=1}^{n}\ker\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j})D^{\mu_{j}}.

Another proof is provided by Horner’s method, which, in effect, expresses ( ​Δ(t1:j):j=1:n)(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j}):j=1{:}n) as linear functions of ( ​Δ(tj)Dμj:j=1:n)(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{j})D^{\mu_{j}}:j=1{:}n), thus showing the first sequence to be contained in the span of the second. Since the first is linearly independent (as it has (wj−1,t:j=1:n)(w_{j-1,t}:j=1{:}n) as a dual sequence) while both contain the same number of terms, it follows that both are bases of the same linear space.       

This proposition provides a ready extension of  ​Δ(t1:n)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n}) to functions more general than polynomials, namely to any function for which the derivatives mentioned in (36) make sense. It is exactly those functions for which the Hermite conditions (33) make sense, hence for which the Hermite interpolant rr of (32) is defined. This leads us to G. Kowalewski’s definition.

Definition 37 ([ citK ])

For any smooth enough function ff defined, at least, at t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n},  ​Δ(t1:n)f\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})f is the leading coefficient, i.e., the coefficient of ()n−1()^{n-1}, in the power form for the Hermite interpolant to ff at t1:nt_{1:n}.

In consequence,  ​Δ(t1:n)f= ​Δ(t1:n)p\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}n})f=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}n})p for any polynomial pp that matches ff at t1:nt_{1{:}n}.

Example 8. Assume that none of the tjt_{j} is zero. Then,

 ​Δ(t1:n)()−1=(−1)n−1/(t1⋯tn).\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})()^{-1}=(-1)^{n-1}/(t_{1}\cdots t_{n}).\immediate (38)

This certainly holds for n=1n=1 while, for n>1n>1, by (29), 0= ​Δ(t1:n)(()−1()1)= ​Δ(t1:n)()−1tn+ ​Δ(t1:n−1)()−10=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})(()^{-1}()^{1})=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})()^{-1}t_{n}+\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n-1})()^{-1}, hence  ​Δ(t1:n)()−1=− ​Δ(t1:n−1)()−1/tn\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})()^{-1}=-\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n-1})()^{-1}/t_{n}, and induction finishes the proof. This implies the handy formula

 ​Δ(t1:n)(z−⋅)−1=1/wn,t(z),z≠t1,…,tn.\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})(z-\cdot)^{-1}=1/w_{n,t}(z),\quad z\not=t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}.\immediate (39)

Therefore, with #ξ:=#{j:ξ=tj,1≤j≤n}\#\xi:=\#\{j:\xi=t_{j},1\leq j\leq n\} the multiplicity with which ξ\xi occurs in the sequence t1:nt_{1:n}, and

1/wn,t​(z)=:∑ξ∈t∑0≤μ<#​ξμ!​Aξ​μ(z−ξ)μ+11/w_{n,t}(z)=:\sum_{\xi\in t}\sum_{0\leq\mu<\#\xi}{\mu!A_{\xi\mu}\over(z-\xi)^{\mu+1}}

the partial fraction expansion of 1/wn,t1/w_{n,t}, we obtain Chakalov’s expansion

 ​Δ​(t0,…,tk)​f=∑ξ∈t∑0≤μ<#​ξAξ​μ​Dμ​f​(ξ)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{0},\ldots,t_{k})f=\sum_{\xi\in t}\sum_{0\leq\mu<\#\xi}A_{\xi\mu}D^{\mu}f(\xi)\immediate (40)

(from [ citCh38 ]) for f:=1/(z−⋅)f:=1/(z-\cdot) for arbitrary zz since Dμ1/(z−⋅)=μ!/(z−⋅)μ+1D^{\mu}1/(z-\cdot)=\mu!/(z-\cdot)^{\mu+1}, hence also for any smooth enough ff, by the density of {1/(z−⋅):z∈IF}\{1/(z-\cdot):z\in{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}\}.

This is an illustration of the peculiar effectiveness of the formula (39), for the divided difference of 1/(z−⋅)1/(z-\cdot), for deriving and verifying divided difference identities.       

Example 9. When the tjt_{j} are pairwise distinct, (40) must reduce to

 ​Δ(t1:n)f=∑j=1nf(tj)/Dwn,t(tj),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n})f=\sum_{j=1}^{n}f(t_{j})/Dw_{n,t}(t_{j}),\immediate (41)

since this is readily seen to be the leading coefficient of the polynomial of degree <n<n that matches a given ff at the nn pairwise distinct sites t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n} when we write that polynomial in Lagrange form,

∑j=1nf(tj)∏i∈1:n\j⋅−titj−ti.\sum_{j=1}^{n}f(t_{j})\prod_{i\in 1{:}n\backslash j}{\cdot-t_{i}\over t_{j}-t_{i}}.

It follows (see the proof of [ citET : Lemma I]) that, for −1≤t1<⋯<tn≤1-1\leq t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}\leq 1,

∥ ​Δ(t1:n):C([−1..1])→IF∥=∑j=1n1/|Dwn,t(tj)|≥2n−2,\|\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n}):C([-1\mathbin{\mathchar 24890\relax\mathchar 24890\relax}1])\to{{\rm I}\kern-1.60004pt{\rm F}}\|=\sum_{j=1}^{n}1/|Dw_{n,t}(t_{j})|\geq 2^{n-2},\immediate (42)

with equality iff wn,t=(()2−1)​Un−2w_{n,t}=(()^{2}-1)U_{n-2}, where Un−2U_{n-2} is the second-kind Chebyshev polynomial.

Indeed, for any such

τ:=(t1,…,tn),\tau:=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}),

the restriction λ\lambda of  ​Δ​(τ)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau) to Π<n\Pi_{<n} is the unique linear functional on Π<n\Pi_{<n} that vanishes on Π<n−1\Pi_{<n-1} and takes the value 11 at ()n−1()^{n-1}, hence takes its norm on the error of the best (uniform) approximation to ()n−1()^{n-1} from Π<n−1\Pi_{<n-1}, i.e., on the Chebyshev polynomial of degree n−1n-1. Each such  ​Δ​(τ)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau) is an extension of this λ\lambda, hence has norm ≥‖λ‖=1/dist(()n−1,Π<n−1)=2n−2\geq\|\lambda\|=1/\mathop{\rm dist}{}(()^{n-1},\Pi_{<n-1})=2^{n-2}, with equality iff  ​Δ​(τ)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau) takes on its norm on that Chebyshev polynomial, i.e., iff τ\tau is the sequence of extreme sites of that Chebyshev polynomial.       

8   The divided difference as approximate normalized derivative

Assume that ff is differentiable on an interval that contains the nondecreasing finite sequence

τ=(τ0≤⋯≤τk),\tau=(\tau_{0}\leq\cdots\leq\tau_{k}),

and assume further that  ​Δ​(τ)​f\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau)f is defined, hence so is the Hermite interpolant

Pτ​fP_{\tau}f

of ff at τ\tau.

Then f−Pτ​ff-P_{\tau}f vanishes at τ0:k\tau_{0{:}k}, therefore D⁡(f−Pτ​f)D(f-P_{\tau}f) vanishes at some σ=(σ0,…,σk−1)\sigma=(\sigma_{0},\ldots,\sigma_{k-1}) that interlaces τ\tau, meaning that

τi≤σi≤τi+1,all​i.\tau_{i}\leq\sigma_{i}\leq\tau_{i+1},\quad{\rm all\ }i.

This is evident when τi=τj\tau_{i}=\tau_{j} for some i<ji<j, and is Rolle’s Theorem when τi<τi+1\tau_{i}<\tau_{i+1}. Consequently, D​Pτ​fDP_{\tau}f is a polynomial of degree <k<k that matches D​fDf at σ0,…,σk−1\sigma_{0},\ldots,\sigma_{k-1}, hence must be its Hermite interpolant at σ\sigma. This proves the following.

Proposition 43 ([ citHo ])

If ff is differentiable on an interval that contains the nondecreasing (k+1)(k+1)-sequence τ\tau and smooth enough at τ\tau so that its Hermite interpolant, Pτ​fP_{\tau}f, at τ\tau exists, then there is a nondecreasing kk-sequence σ\sigma interlacing τ\tau and so that

Pσ​(D​f)=D​Pτ​f.P_{\sigma}(Df)=DP_{\tau}f.

In particular, then

k​ ​Δ​(τ)​f= ​Δ​(σ)​D​f.k\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau)f=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\sigma)Df.

From this, induction provides the

Corollary ([ citSc ])

Under the same assumptions, but with ff kk times differentiable on that interval, there exists ξ\xi in that interval for which

k!​ ​Δ​(τ0,…,τk)=Dk​f​(ξ).k!\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau_{0},\ldots,\tau_{k})=D^{k}f(\xi).\immediate (44)

The special case k=1k=1, i.e.,

 ​Δ​(a,b)​f=D​f​(ξ),for some ​ξ∈(a..b),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(a,b)f=Df(\xi),\quad\hbox{for\ some\ }\xi\in(a\mathbin{\mathchar 24890\relax\mathchar 24890\relax}b),

is so obvious a consequence or restatement of L’Hôpital’s Rule, it must have been around at least that long.

Chakalov [ citCh34 ] has made a detailed study of the possible values that ξ\xi might take in (44) as ff varies over a given class of functions.

[ citKA : p. 91] reports that already Taylor, in [ citT ], derived his eponymous expansion (13) as the limit of Newton’s formula, albeit for equally spaced sites only.

9   Representations

Determinant ratio.  Let

τ:=(τ0,…,τk).\tau:=(\tau_{0},\ldots,\tau_{k}).

Kowalewski’s definition of  ​Δ​(τ)​f\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau)f as the leading coefficient, in the power form, of the Hermite interpolant to ff at τ\tau gives, for the case of simple sites and via Cramer’s Rule, the formula

 ​Δ​(τ)​f=detQτ​[()0,…,()k−1,f]/detQτ​[()0,…,()k]\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau)f\;=\;\det Q_{\tau}[()^{0},\ldots,()^{k-1},f]/\det Q_{\tau}[()^{0},\ldots,()^{k}]\immediate (45)

in which

Qτ[g0,…,gk]:=(gj(τi):i,j=0,…,k).Q_{\tau}[g_{0},\ldots,g_{k}]:=(g_{j}(\tau_{i}):i,j=0,\ldots,k).

In some papers and books, the identity (45) serves as the definition of  ​Δ​(τ)​f\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau)f despite the fact that it needs awkward modification in the case of repeated sites.

Peano kernel (B-spline).  Assume that τ:=(τ0,…,τk)\tau:=(\tau_{0},\ldots,\tau_{k}) lies in the interval [a..b][a\mathbin{\mathchar 24890\relax\mathchar 24890\relax}b] and that ff has kk derivatives on that interval. Then, on that interval, we have Taylor’s identity

f⁡(x)=∑j<k(x−a)j​Dj​f​(a)/j!+∫ab(x−y)+k−1​Dk​f​(y)​𝑑y/(k−1)!.f(x)=\sum_{j<k}(x-a)^{j}D^{j}f(a)/j!+\int_{a}^{b}(x-y)_{+}^{k-1}D^{k}f(y)\,{\rm d}y/(k-1)!.\immediate (46)

If now τ0<τk\tau_{0}<\tau_{k}, then, from Proposition 35,  ​Δ​(τ)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau) is a weighted sum of values of derivatives of order <k<k, hence commutes with the integral in Taylor’s formula (46) while, in any case, it annihilates any polynomial of degree <k<k. Therefore

 ​Δ(τ)f=∫abM(⋅|τ)Dkf/k!,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau)f=\int_{a}^{b}M(\cdot|\tau)D^{k}f/k!,\immediate (47)

with

M(x|τ):=k ​Δ(τ)(⋅−x)+k−1M(x|\tau):=k\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau)(\cdot-x)_{+}^{k-1}\immediate (48)

the Curry-Schoenberg B-spline (see [ citCS ]) with knots τ\tau and normalized to have integral 1. While Schoenberg and Curry named and studied the B-spline only in the 1940’s, it appears in this role as the Peano kernel for the divided difference already earlier, e.g., in [ citP33 ] and [ citCh34 ] (see [ citBP ]) or [ citFa ].

Contour integral.  An entirely different approach to divided differences and Hermite interpolation begins with Frobenius’ paper [ citFr ], so different that it had no influence on the literature on interpolation (except for a footnote-like mention in [ citCh38 ]). To be sure, Frobenius himself seems to have thought of it more as an exercise in expansions, never mentioning the word ‘interpolation’. Nevertheless, Frobenius describes in full detail the salient facts of polynomial interpolation in the complex case, with the aid of the Cauchy integral.

In [ citFr ], Frobenius investigates Newton series, i.e., infinite expansions

∑j=1∞cj​wj−1,t\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}c_{j}w_{j-1,t}

in the Newton polynomials wj,tw_{j,t} defined in (2). He begins with the identity

(y−x)​∑j=1nwj−1,t​(x)wj,t​(y)= 1−wn,t​(x)wn,t​(y),(y-x)\sum_{j=1}^{n}{w_{j-1,t}(x)\over w_{j,t}(y)}\;=\;1-{w_{n,t}(x)\over w_{n,t}(y)},\immediate (49)

a ready consequence of the observations

x​wj−1,t​(x)=wj,t​(x)+tj​wj−1,t​(x),ywj,t​(y)=1wj−1,t​(y)+tjwj−1,t​(y)\eqalign{xw_{j-1,t}(x)\;&\;=\;w_{j,t}(x)\;\;+\;\;t_{j}w_{j-1,t}(x),\cr\vskip 2.0pt\cr{y\over w_{j,t}(y)}\;&\;=\;\;{1\over w_{j-1,t}(y)}\;\;+\;\;{t_{j}\over w_{j-1,t}(y)}\cr}

since these imply that

y​∑j=1nwj−1,t​(x)wj,t​(y)=∑jwj−1,t​(x)wj−1,t​(y)+∑jtj​wj−1,t​(x)wj,t​(y),x​∑j=1nwj−1,t​(x)wj,t​(y)=∑jwj,t​(x)wj,t​(y)+∑jtj​wj−1,t​(x)wj,t​(y).\eqalign{y\sum_{j=1}^{n}{w_{j-1,t}(x)\over w_{j,t}(y)}\;=\;&\sum_{j}{w_{j-1,t}(x)\over w_{j-1,t}(y)}+\sum_{j}{t_{j}w_{j-1,t}(x)\over w_{j,t}(y)},\cr\vskip 2.0pt\cr x\sum_{j=1}^{n}{w_{j-1,t}(x)\over w_{j,t}(y)}\;=\;&\sum_{j}{w_{j,t}(x)\over w_{j,t}(y)}+\sum_{j}{t_{j}w_{j-1,t}(x)\over w_{j,t}(y)}.\cr}

Then (in §4), he uses (49), in the form

∑j=1nwj−1,t​(z)wj,t​(ζ)+wn,t​(z)(ζ−z)​wn,t​(ζ)= 1/(ζ−z),\sum_{j=1}^{n}{w_{j-1,t}(z)\over w_{j,t}(\zeta)}+{w_{n,t}(z)\over(\zeta-z)w_{n,t}(\zeta)}\;=\;1/(\zeta-z),

in Cauchy’s formula

f⁡(z)=12​π​i​∮f⁡(ζ)​d​ζζ−zf(z)={1\over 2\pi{\rm i}}\oint{f(\zeta)\,{\rm d}\zeta\over\zeta-z}

to conclude that

f⁡(z)=∑j=1nwj−1,t​cj+wn,t​12​π​i​∮f⁡(ζ)​d​ζ(ζ−z)​wn,t​(ζ),f(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j-1,t}c_{j}\;+\;w_{n,t}{1\over 2\pi{\rm i}}\oint{f(\zeta)\,{\rm d}\zeta\over(\zeta-z)w_{n,t}(\zeta)},\immediate (50)

with

cj:=12​π​i∮f⁡(ζ)​d​ζwj,t​(ζ),j=1,…,n.c_{j}\;:=\;{1\over 2\pi{\rm i}}\oint{f(\zeta)\,{\rm d}\zeta\over w_{j,t}(\zeta)},\quad j=1,\ldots,n.

For this, he assumes that zz is in some disk of radius ρ\rho, in which ff is entire, and ζ\zeta runs on the boundary of a disk of radius ρ′<ρ\rho^{\prime}<\rho that contains zz, with none of the relevant tjt_{j} in the annulus formed by the two disks.

Directly from the definition of the divided difference, we therefore conclude that, under these assumptions on ff and tt,

 ​Δ(t1:j)f=12​π​i∮f⁡(ζ)​d​ζwj,t​(ζ),j=0,1,2,….\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1{:}j})f\;=\;{1\over 2\pi{\rm i}}\oint{f(\zeta)\,{\rm d}\zeta\over w_{j,t}(\zeta)},\quad j=0,1,2,\ldots.\immediate (51)

Strikingly, Frobenius never mentions that (50) provides a general polynomial interpolant and its error. Could he have been unaware of it? To be sure, he could not have called it ‘Hermite interpolation’ since Hermite’s paper [ citH78 ] appeared well after Frobenius’. There is no indication that Hermite was aware of Frobenius’ paper.

Genocchi-Hermite.  Starting with (19) and the observation that

 ​Δ​(x,y)​f=∫01D​f​((1−s)​x+s​y)​𝑑s,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(x,y)f=\int_{0}^{1}Df((1-s)x+sy)\,{\rm d}s,

induction on nn gives the (univariate) Genocchi-Hermite formula

 ​Δ​(τ0,…,τn)​f=∫[τ0,…,τn]Dn​f,\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\tau_{0},\ldots,\tau_{n})f=\int_{[\tau_{0},\ldots,\tau_{n}]}D^{n}f,\immediate (52)

with

∫[τ0,…,τn]f:=∫01∫0s1⋯∫0sn−1f((1−s1)τ0+⋯+(sn−1−sn)τn−1+snτn)dsn⋯ds1.\eqalign{\int_{[\tau_{0},\ldots,\tau_{n}]}f\;:=\;&\cr&\kern-56.9055pt\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{s_{1}}\cdots\int_{0}^{s_{n-1}}f((1-s_{1})\tau_{0}+\cdots+(s_{n-1}-s_{n})\tau_{n-1}+s_{n}\tau_{n})\,{\rm d}s_{n}\cdots\,{\rm d}s_{1}.\cr}

[ citNo : p.16] mistakenly attributes (52) to [ citH59 ], possibly because that paper carries the suggestive title “Sur l’interpolation”.

At the end of the paper [ citH78 ], on polynomial interpolation to data at the nn pairwise distinct sites t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n} in the complex plane, Hermite does give a formula involving the righthand-side of the above, namely the formula

f(x)−Pf(x)=(x−t1)⋯(x−tn)∫[tn,…,t1,x]Dnff(x)-Pf(x)=(x-t_{1})\cdots(x-t_{n})\int_{[t_{n},\ldots,t_{1},x]}D^{n}f

for the error in the Lagrange interpolant P​fPf to ff at t1:nt_{1:n}. Thus, it requires the observation that

f(x)−Pf(x)=(x−t1)⋯(x−tn) ​Δ(tn,…,t1,x)ff(x)-Pf(x)=(x-t_{1})\cdots(x-t_{n})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{n},\ldots,t_{1},x)f

to deduce the Genocchi-Hermite formula from [ citH78 ]. (He also gives the rather more complicated formula

f⁡(x)−P​f​(x)=(x−a1)α⋯(x−an)λ∫[an,…,a1,x][[sn−sn−1]]α−1⋯[[1−s1]]λ−1Dα+⋯+λf\eqalign{f(x)-Pf(x)=&\cr&\kern-56.9055pt(x-a_{1})^{\alpha}\cdots(x-a_{n})^{\lambda}\int_{[a_{n},\ldots,a_{1},x]}\hbox{$[\![$}s_{n}-s_{n-1}\hbox{$]\!]$}^{\alpha-1}\cdots\hbox{$[\![$}1-s_{1}\hbox{$]\!]$}^{\lambda-1}D^{\alpha+\cdots+\lambda}f\cr}

for the error in case of repeated interpolation. Here, [[​z​]]j:=zj/j!\hbox{$[\![$}z\hbox{$]\!]$}^{j}:=z^{j}/j!.)

In contrast, [ citG69 ] is explicitly concerned with a representation formula for the divided difference. However, the ‘divided difference’ he represents is the following:

 ​Δ(x,x+h1) ​Δ(⋅,⋅+h2)⋯ ​Δ(⋅,⋅+hn)=(Δh1/h1)⋯(Δhn/hn)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(x,x+h_{1})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\cdot,\cdot+h_{2})\cdots\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\cdot,\cdot+h_{n})=(\Delta_{h_{1}}/h_{1})\cdots(\Delta_{h_{n}}/h_{n})

and for it he gets the representation

∫01⋯∫01Dnf(x+h1t1+⋯+hntn)dt1⋯dtn.\int_{0}^{1}\cdots\int_{0}^{1}D^{n}f(x+h_{1}t_{1}+\cdots+h_{n}t_{n})\,{\rm d}t_{1}\cdots\,{\rm d}t_{n}.

[ citNo : p.16] cites [ citG78a ], [ citG78b ] as places where formulations equivalent to the Genocchi-Hermite formula can be found. So far, I’ve been only able to find [ citG78b ]. It is a letter to Hermite, in which Genocchi brings, among other things, the above representation formula to Hermite’s attention, refers to a paper of his in [Archives de Grunert, t. XLIX, 3e cahier] as containing a corresponding error formula for Newton interpolation. He states that he, in continuing work, had obtained such a representation also for Ampère’s fonctions interpolatoires (aka divided differences), and finishes with the formula

∫01⋅⋅∫01s1n−1s2n−2⋯sn−1Dnf(x0+s1(x1−x0)+⋯+s1s2⋯sn(xn−xn−1))ds1⋯dsn\eqalign{\int_{0}^{1}\cdot\cdot\int_{0}^{1}s_{1}^{n-1}s_{2}^{n-2}\cdots s_{n-1}&\cr&\kern-71.13188ptD^{n}f(x_{0}+s_{1}(x_{1}-x_{0})+\cdots+s_{1}s_{2}\cdots s_{n}(x_{n}-x_{n-1}))\,{\rm d}s_{1}\cdots\,{\rm d}s_{n}\cr}

for  ​Δ​(x0,…,xn)​f\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(x_{0},\ldots,x_{n})f, and says that it is equivalent to the formula

 ​Δ(x0,…,xn)f=∫⋯∫Dnf(s0x0+s1x1+⋯snxn)ds1⋯dsn\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(x_{0},\ldots,x_{n})f=\int\cdots\int D^{n}f(s_{0}x_{0}+s_{1}x_{1}+\cdots s_{n}x_{n})\,{\rm d}s_{1}\cdots\,{\rm d}s_{n}

in which the conditions s0+⋯+sn=1s_{0}+\cdots+s_{n}=1, si≥0s_{i}\geq 0, all ii, are imposed.

[ citSt27 : p.17f] proves the Genocchi-Hermite formula but calls it Jensen’s formula, because of [ citJ ].

10   Divided difference expansions of the divided difference

By applying  ​Δ(s1:m)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:m}) to both sides of the identity

 ​Δ(⋅)=∑j=1nwj−1,t ​Δ(t1:j)+wn,t ​Δ(t1:n,⋅)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(\cdot)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j-1,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})+w_{n,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n},\cdot)

obtained from (16), one obtains the expansion

 ​Δ(s1:m)=∑j=mn ​Δ(s1:m)wj−1,t ​Δ(t1:j)+E(s,t),\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:m})=\sum_{j=m}^{n}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:m})w_{j-1,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})+E(s,t),

where, by the Leibniz formula (29),

E⁡(s,t):=Δ(s1:m)(wn,tΔ(t1:n,⋅))=∑i=1mΔ(si:m)wn,tΔ(s1:m,t1:n).\eqalign{E(s,t):=\;&\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:m})(w_{n,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:n},\cdot))\cr=\;&\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{i:m})w_{n,t}\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:m},t_{1:n}).}

But, following [ citFl ] and with p:=n−mp:=n-m, one gets the better formula

E(s,t):=∑i=1m(si−ti+p)( ​Δ(s1:i)wi+p,t) ​Δ(t1:i+p,si:m)E(s,t):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(s_{i}-t_{i+p})(\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:i})w_{i+p,t})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:i+p},s_{i:m})

in which all the divided differences on the right side are of the same order, nn. The proof (see [ citB03 ]), by induction on nn, uses the easy consequence of (29) that

(si−y) ​Δ(si:m)f= ​Δ(si:m)((⋅−y)f)− ​Δ(si+1:m)f.(s_{i}-y)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{i:m})f=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{i:m})((\cdot-y)f)-\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{i+1:m})f.

The induction is anchored at n=mn=m for which the formula

 ​Δ(s1:m)− ​Δ(t1:m)=∑i=1m(si−ti) ​Δ(s1:i,ti:m)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:m})-\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:m})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(s_{i}-t_{i})\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(s_{1:i},t_{i:m})

can already be found in [ citHo ].

11   Notation and nomenclature

It is quite common in earlier literature to use the notation

[y1,…,yj][y_{1},\ldots,y_{j}]

for the divided difference of order j−1j-1 of data ((ti,yi):i=1:j)((t_{i},y_{i}):i=1{:}j). This reflects the fact that divided differences were thought of as convenient expressions in terms of the given data rather than as linear functionals on some vector space of functions.

The presently most common notation for  ​Δ(t1:j)p= ​Δ(t1,…,tj)p\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1:j})p=\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{j})p is

p⁡[t1,…,tj]p[t_{1},\ldots,t_{j}]

(or, perhaps, p⁡(t1,…,tj)p(t_{1},\ldots,t_{j})) which enlarges upon the fact that  ​Δ​(z)​p=p​(z)\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}(z)p=p(z), but this becomes awkward when the divided difference is to be treated as a linear functional. In that regard, the notation

[t1,…,tj]​p[t_{1},\ldots,t_{j}]p

is better, but suffers from the fact that the resulting notation

[t1,…,tj][t_{1},\ldots,t_{j}]

for the linear functional itself conflicts with standard notations, such as the matrix (or, more generally, the column map) with columns t1,…,tjt_{1},\ldots,t_{j}, or, in the special case j=2j=2, i.e.,

[t1,t2],[t_{1},t_{2}],

the closed interval with endpoints t1t_{1} and t2t_{2} or else the scalar product of the vectors t1t_{1} and t2t_{2}. The notation

[t1,…,tj;p][t_{1},\ldots,t_{j};p]

does not suffer from this defect, as it leads to the notation [t1,…,tj;⋅][t_{1},\ldots,t_{j};\cdot] for the linear functional itself, though it requires the reader not to mistakenly read that semicolon as yet another comma.

The notation,  ​Δ\mathord{\kern 4.29993pt\vrule width=0.6pt,height=5.6pt,depth=-0.28pt\kern-4.19998pt\Delta}, used in this essay was proposed by W. Kahan some time ago (see, e.g., [ citKa ]), and does not suffer from any of the defects mentioned and has the advantage of being literal (given that Δ\Delta is standard notation for a difference). Here is a TeX macro for it:

\def\divdif{\mathord\kern.43em\vrule width.6pt height5.6pt \def\divdif{\ depth-.28pt \kern-.43em\Delta}

Although divided differences are rightly associated with Newton (because of [ citN87 : Book iii, Lemma v, Case ii], [ citN11 ]; for a detailed discussion, including facsimiles of the originals and their translations, see [ citFra18 ], [ citFra19 ], [ citFra27 ]), the term ‘divided difference’ was, according to [ citWR : p.20], first used in [ citM : p.550], even though, by then, Ampère [ citA ] had called it fonction interpolaire, and this is the term used in the French literature of the 1800s. To be sure, in [ citN11 ], Newton repeatedly uses the term “differentia sic divisa’.
